entities.name: William III of Cagliari
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William III of Cagliari, also known by his baptismal name Guglielmo Cepolla or Cipolla, was the final indigenous ruler of the Judicate of Cagliari, one of the four independent Sardinian states in the medieval period. Reigning briefly as Salusio VI from 1256 until his deposition in 1258, his tenure marked the definitive end of Sardinian judicial autonomy in the southern part of the island, an era spanning over four centuries. His fall represented the culmination of intense Pisan and Genoese mercantile and military pressures, alongside internal dynastic strife, dramatically reshaping the political landscape of Sardinia by fragmenting the judicate.

Ascending to power through a popular revolt against the Pisan-backed Gherardo della Gherardesca, who had claimed the Judicate after the death of the childless Judge Giovanni (Chiano) Visconti, William III initially sought to reassert Sardinian sovereignty. He adopted the traditional enthronement name Salusio VI, signaling a return to local rule. However, his brief reign was characterized by a desperate struggle against the formidable economic and military might of the Republic of Pisa. Pisa, eager to solidify its control over the lucrative mineral resources and strategic ports of southern Sardinia, launched a decisive military campaign in 1258, besieging the capital Santa Igia and ultimately destroying it.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: William III's brief reign marks the definitive end of the independent Judicate of Cagliari, a state that had existed for over four centuries. His defeat in 1258 directly led to the fragmentation and Pisan control of southern Sardinia, fundamentally altering the island's political landscape until the Aragonese conquest.
